1:
Whether this is a psalm at all, or the tail of the one before, is the first question. Calvin reports that most critics take the two as originally one, that forty-six manuscripts still print them so, and that the similarity of style, sentiment and metre, with the recurring refrain, confirms it; he passes on Williams's explanation, that the Jewish choristers, finding the anthem too long, divided it for their own convenience — no uncommon thing among choristers — and that once divided it was ignorantly supposed it ought to be. Clarke counts the same manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, notes that Hebrew and Chaldee give it no title, and reports two that others supply: the Syriac, that David composed it when Jonathan told him Saul intended to slay him, and the Arabic, that it is a prayer for the backsliding Jews. His own judgment is that it continues the complaint of the captive Jews in Babylon.

Who the enemies were divides them sharply. Clarke names them outright — the ungodly nation is the Babylonians, impious and perfidious, and the deceitful and unjust man is Nebuchadnezzar. Calvin has David driven out of his own country by the violence and tyranny of his enemies, calling upon God for vengeance and encouraging himself to hope for restoration. Wesley takes the nation for the sheer number of David's adversaries and guesses the man to be Ahithophel or Absalom; Henry inclines to Saul, who not only showed David no kindness but dealt dishonestly with him. Ellicott works on the word instead: in the Hebrew it is simply a negative term, a nation not in the covenant, though naturally a positive idea of ungodliness would come to attach to it.

Henry reads the opening plea as two lawsuits at once. Against those who impeached him David is defendant, and from their courts, where he stood unjustly convicted, he appeals to the court of heaven, praying to have their judgment reversed and his innocence cleared; against those who injured him he is plaintiff, exhibiting his complaint to the avenger of wrong. He notes what the word unmerciful implies: those who are unmerciful show themselves ungodly, since anyone with fear or love of the master will have compassion on his fellow-servants. Spurgeon takes the appeal as a willingness to be examined: others cannot understand my motives and will not give me a just verdict, but my heart is clear as to its intent, and I am content that God should weigh my character. If he judges, his acceptance is enough, and human misrepresentation may be laughed at. One such advocate will more than suffice to answer a nation of brawling accusers; one good word from God outweighs ten thousand railing speeches of men, and the arrows of calumny fall harmlessly from the shield of a man whose reliance is upon his God. Clarke adds that the phrase is forensic, rightly rendered plead my cause — be my counsellor and advocate; Gill notes the Targum's addition, with the judgment of truth.

Augustine takes the hunger of the psalm literally and then not. It is a short psalm, he says, satisfying the mental cravings of its hearers without imposing too severe a trial on those fasting; and the soul it calls cast down is cast down from some hunger, for fasting is voluntary but being an-hungered is not. What is an-hungered is the Church, that Man extended through the whole world whose Head is above and whose limbs are below — his voice, now chanting joyously and now sorrowing, so that we need not be told who speaks here if each of us is a member of that Body. On the plea itself he is unafraid: I do not dread thy judgment, because I know thy mercy. Yet in this pilgrimage the separation asked for is not yet granted, since he must live with the tares until the harvest.
2:
The complaint and the confidence rest on one ground. Gill points out that the God addressed as the psalmist's strength is able to deliver as well as to plead his cause, being the giver of strength natural and spiritual, and the strength of his heart, life and salvation — reason enough for committing the cause to him. Clarke keeps the plural sense he has argued throughout, hearing the captives speak: we still acknowledge thee for our God, so why are we cast off, and now that we are humbled and penitent, why are we not saved from this oppression?

What is asked for is an escort home. Ellicott draws the contrast that gives the petition its force: instead of the contemptuous guard who had led the exile away from the holy hill, the poet prays that God's light and truth may lead him back, like two angel guides — light and truth, he exclaims, what a guidance in this world of falsehood and shadow, the Urim and Thummim of the saints, escorting all faithful souls in every age. Clarke reads the two as answering the halves of the trouble: we are in darkness, so send light; we look for the fulfilment of thy promises, so send forth thy truth — one to guide us to the country of our fathers, the other to thy tabernacles. Wesley glosses the sending as an actual discovery of them, and takes the truth for God's favour and his promises, or the illumination of his Spirit and the direction of his providence. Gill opens the light three ways before choosing — the Messiah, whom some Jewish interpreters find here; the Spirit; or the Gospel — though he thinks the light of God's countenance likelier, the discoveries of favour which produce life, joy and peace; and the truth he takes for Christ, or the word of truth, or rather God's faithfulness.

Where the light is to lead the fourth verse answers, and the answer is an altar. Gill sets it in the tabernacle, whether of burnt offering or of incense, adding that under the Gospel the altar is Christ. Clarke keeps the exile's sequence — when thy light has led us back, and thy truth set us again at the door of thy tabernacles, then will we go to thy altar and offer joyfully what thy law requires. Spurgeon presses past the furniture to what it is for. If David were granted a deliverance that let him return, it is not his own house that his willing feet would seek first but the altar, counting it his greatest happiness to lie there as a burnt offering wholly dedicated. Yet it was not the altar as such he cared for, being no believer in ritualism: what are the rites of worship unless the Lord be in them, but empty shells and dry husks? Note the rapture of the title — God is not his joy only but his exceeding joy, not the fountain or giver of joy but that joy itself, the margin having it the gladness of my joy. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same movement as anticipation: the poet revels beforehand in what he has prayed for, knowing no joy like that which proceeds from God, and no higher aim than to be again where its fountainhead is, and where it flows forth in streams. Ellicott notes only that the closing title, God my God, is the form this collection uses for the more usual Jehovah my God.

On the refrain that ends the psalm Clarke turns the delay into an argument for patience. Though our deliverance be put off, God has not forgotten to be gracious; the word concerning the captivity was for an appointed time, and though it appear to tarry we must wait, since in the end it will come and will not tarry. Why then should we be discouraged?
